To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) making an error of commission oneself, compared to hearing another person make the error, is beneficial for later recall; (b) generating a correct answer, oneself, outloud, compared to hearing someone else give a correct answer, is beneficial for subsequent recall; and (c) being "on-the hook" for a correct response is beneficial for subsequent memory of the correct answer.

(1) self-generation of errors of commission and self-generation of correct responses, compared to other-generation (of either correct responses or errors), is associated with greater later recall of the target item, and (2) this benefit is fragile and may be attenuated by the presence of other participants.

(a) self-generation of either correct or incorrect responses enhances later recall of those responses; (b) self-generation is beneficial even when the self-generated response was incorrect; and (c) self-generation is not beneficial when another person is generating responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the special role of retrieval as a memory process and its role in the reconsolidation and strengthening of the retrieved trace.
the special status of retrieval, as opposed to encoding, as a memory process.
the role of self-generation, as opposed to other-generation, in learning and memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the case where the person was correct but did not generate the response, there was no benefit, and for the case where they were incorrect and did generate the response, the benefit was substantial, but the benefit was fragile.

the benefit of generating errors oneself (as compared to hearing someone else generate an error) is a robust effect, whereas the effect of being "on-the hook" as compared to not being "on-the-hoook" is fragile.
the benefits of self-generation are not robust to all manipulations, but that the benefits of being "on the hook" are robust to the manipulations we have tested.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the benefit of self-generation is robust, and that the effect of being on the hook is fragile.
self-generated errors are beneficial for memory, and that this benefit is mediated by the special molarability of the retrieved traces.

the benefits of self-generation are due to the fact that self-generated information is more likely to be retrieved in the future, and the benefits of error-generation are due to a combination of factors, including the benefits of self-generated information, but also due to the fact, as we argue in the paper, that the error-generation process is more likely than correct-generation to result in a change in the representation of the memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to distinguish between the effects of generating a correct response, generating an incorrect response, and not generating any response at all.
it is the retrieval process itself, not the content of what is retrieved, which makes it possible to correct errors.
, if the learner is the agent of the retrieval, then the retrieval process is beneficial, whether or not the retrieved trace is correct.
